label: Newspaper abstracts only
basis: 76 rows of record_type=newspaper in loudoun_deaths.csv; years present 1818, 1819, 1820, 1821.
source: loudoun_deaths.csv (src_page 100-104; Genius of Liberty, The Washingtonian)
note: The earliest documentary layer in the project. Newspaper death notices only, which means the wealthy, the notable and the violently killed. Not a population record.

label: No source IN THIS PROJECT (newspapers exist)
basis: Zero rows in loudoun_deaths.csv fall in 1822-1852. The newspaper abstracts stop at 1821 and the state register does not begin until 1853.
note: CORRECTED 26 Oct 2026. Seven people total die in the 1830s and 1840s in this dataset, and loudoun_deaths.csv holds nothing at all for 1822-1852. BUT THAT IS A GAP IN THIS PROJECT'S EXTRACTION, NOT IN THE SURVIVING RECORD: the Genius of Liberty (Leesburg) is digitised for 1817-1839 with 1,178 issues, and the Leesburg Genius of Liberty for 1839-1843 with 179 more. See loudoun_papers.csv. THE TRUE DOCUMENTARY VOID FOR LOUDOUN NEWSPAPERS IS 1844-1874 - thirty-one years with no digitised Loudoun paper at all, covering the entire Civil War. 75 people in this project die in that void.

label: No Loudoun newspaper digitised
basis: The Leesburg Genius of Liberty ends 20 May 1843; the Mirror (Leesburg) does not begin until 7 January 1875. No digitised Loudoun title covers the span between. See loudoun_papers.csv.
source: Virginia Chronicle title records for all 12 Loudoun publications
note: THIRTY-ONE YEARS, AND IT SWALLOWS THE CIVIL WAR AND THE BURNING RAID. 75 people in this project die inside it. This void overlaps the state death register (1853-1866), which is why that register is the only substantial source for the period and why its 1860-1863 gap is so damaging - for those four years there is neither a register nor a newspaper.

label: Virginia state death register
basis: 1,403 rows of record_type=register. Years present 1853-1859 and 1864-1866.
note: The richest layer in the project: cause of death, parents, birthplace, informant. Also the most silent - 0 of 1,403 entries mark a Black decedent, in a county that was 31 percent Black in 1860. Note that a year-block is the year of the RETURN, so the 1858 block contains Jan-Feb 1859 deaths.

label: Register gap (Civil War)
basis: No register entry in loudoun_deaths.csv carries a year of 1860, 1861, 1862 or 1863.
note: Four consecutive years absent from the state register, covering secession and the first three years of the war. The register resumes in 1864. This gap is the single most misleading stretch of the timeline and must be shown as a gap in the SOURCE, never as a gap in deaths.

label: Virginia state death register resumes
basis: Register entries present for 1864, 1865 and 1866, then the record type ends.
note: Includes the Burning Raid winter of 1864-65. No death in the register is attributable to the raid.

label: Private death lists
basis: 338 rows of record_type=deathlist. Burr W. Paxson's list via John A. Divine of Waterford (1868-1892) and John James Dillon's list, Purcellville (1892-1900). Year 1887 absent.
note: Two private compilations standing in for an absent state record. ALL THIRTEEN RACIAL MARKINGS IN THE ENTIRE PROJECT ARE IN THESE LISTS, all post-emancipation. The register's silence was a choice these compilers did not make.

label: 1948 stone survey
basis: 744 rows in timeline_people.csv carry stone_1948.
note: A one-time transcription of standing stones. Captures only the marked graves, and only those still legible in 1948 - it is the reason lost and moved stones leave no trace after this point.

label: Modern online memorial records
basis: The bulk of timeline_people.csv's 2,732 records. Deaths per decade sit between 150 and 215 from the 1900s onward, against 2 to 83 before 1900.
note: Coverage becomes effectively complete here. The flat plateau from 1900 onward is the signature of a complete record; the climb from 1830 to 1900 is the signature of an incomplete one.

label: Rural electrification
basis: Rural Electrification Administration created 11 May 1935; electricity reached Loudoun farms over the following decade.
note: End boundary is an estimate. The specific year Hamilton and the surrounding farms were energised has not been established from a source and should not be asserted.

label: No public school system in Virginia
basis: Virginia funded schooling through the Literary Fund (account established 1811; 1818 act set aside $45,000 a year for educating the poor) administered by county school commissioners, not through a school system. Loudoun reportedly had 75 schools for 900 poor children in 1831, open 70 days a year. In February 1846 Loudoun voted against establishing public schools.
source: Library of Virginia, UncommonWealth, Virginia's Literary Fund; Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)
note: COVERS THE ENTIRE SCHOOLING OF ALL 23 CONFEDERATES IN THIS PROJECT (born 1810-1845) and of everyone buried here who died before about 1930. They were taught in private academies, old-field and subscription schools, and Quaker schools. Enrollment records for these mostly do not survive and are not digitised, which is why no classmate relationships can be established. Any claim the app makes about schooling in this era must be hedged to the institution type, never to a named school.

label: Black education criminalised in Virginia
basis: After Nat Turner's revolt the 1831-32 Virginia legislature barred enslaved and free Black people from assembling to read, write, or hear a Black preacher. The Freedmen's Bureau opened Loudoun headquarters at Leesburg and Middleburg in March 1865.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)
note: Thirty-four years in which schooling Black children in this county was against the law. Individual slaveholders defied it - William Benton, who held 19 people in 1850 and taught them to read and write, and Margaret Harrison Benton of New Lisbon, now Huntland, about four miles northwest of Middleburg - but no institution could. A separate and UNVERIFIED note records eight Black men and women at Waterford listed as literate in the 1850 census. The project holds no records of Black residents from this era at all.

label: Freedmen's Bureau schooling
basis: Bureau headquarters at Leesburg and Middleburg from March 1865; schools at Middleburg and near Hillsboro by January 1866, Lincoln ('Janney's School') and Waterford 1866, two in Leesburg 1866, Waterford built 1867, Willisville 1868. The Bureau closed its Loudoun offices in 1868. By March 1869 seven schools educated Black children in the county, one of them at 'Harmony' - today's Hamilton.
source: Loudoun County Historical Society, 'Timeline of Important African American Events in Loudoun County' (loudounhistory.org)
note: The first schooling available to Black residents of this county, and it predates the public system. The Harmony school is the single most locally relevant row in the education layer: see context_events.csv, 1869-03.

label: Before germ theory
basis: 1,209 cause-of-death entries, overwhelmingly concentrated in the register period. 141 dysentery entries, every one between 1853 and 1866. Consumption, croup, typhoid and 'inflammation' dominate.
source: loudoun_deaths.csv cause field; context_events.csv medical layer
note: Causes in this era name symptoms, not pathogens. The vocabulary itself is a historical artefact and should not be silently modernised.

label: Bacteriology and sanitation
basis: Chlorination of a US public water supply began 26 Sep 1908 (Jersey City). Waterborne typhoid and dysentery collapse across this span.
note: The diseases that fill this project's cause-of-death field become survivable or preventable here. The project has almost no cause data in this era, so the change is visible only in the national record, not in the burials.

label: Antibiotics
basis: Only 17 records in timeline_people.csv carry a cause of death at all; the field is effectively empty after the register period.
note: CAUSE OF DEATH IS UNAVAILABLE FOR THIS ENTIRE ERA in the project's data. Any medical narrative after 1935 rests on the national event layer, not on the people buried here.

label: Slavery
basis: In 1860 Loudoun held 5,501 enslaved and 1,251 free Black people, 31 percent of the county. 0 of 1,403 register entries 1853-1866 mark a Black decedent.
source: context_demography.csv (census via Loudoun Museum); loudoun_deaths.csv racial-marking audit
note: Ends with the 13th Amendment. The project documents essentially none of the people held in slavery in this county - the absence is the historical fact, and the app should say so rather than render an empty band.

label: No high school for Black students in Loudoun
basis: Douglass High School, Leesburg, opened September 1941 as the first high school for African American students in Loudoun County. Before that the only secondary option was the upper level of the Loudoun County Training School.
source: Douglass High School (Leesburg, VA); LCPS Douglass Community Center history
note: EVERY BLACK PERSON IN THE PLEASANT VALLEY RECORDS BORN BEFORE ROUGHLY 1925 HAD NO HIGH SCHOOL AVAILABLE TO THEM IN THIS COUNTY. This era bounds any claim the app makes about education.

label: Reconstruction
basis: 13th Amendment ratified 6 Dec 1865; 14th 9 Jul 1868; 15th 3 Feb 1870.
note: The only window in this timeline between emancipation and disfranchisement in which Black men in Virginia could register and vote freely.

label: The Great Migration out of Loudoun
basis: Loudoun's Black population fell in every decade from 1900 to 1950: 5,868 / 5,221 / 4,810 / 4,347 / 4,094 / 3,976. Steepest drop 1900-1910 (-11.0%); second steepest 1920-1930 (-9.6%). From 31.0% of the county in 1860 to about 10% by the early 20th century.
source: Loudoun Museum, 'From Loudoun to Montclair'; Loudoun County African-American Historic Architectural Resources Survey p.16
note: THE SINGLE LARGEST DEMOGRAPHIC FACT IN THIS PROJECT'S PERIOD, and it runs the opposite way to the burial record: documented burials at Pleasant Valley RISE across exactly the decades when the living Black population FELL. The raw counts understate the outflow because they ignore natural increase. Principal destination Montclair, New Jersey, seeded by labour recruitment from 1870. Push factors documented: the 1902 constitution, the Racial Integrity Act of 1924, the Public Assemblages Act of 1926, and underfunded, overcrowded, unsafe Black schools - Loudoun had no Black high school until 1941.

label: Disfranchisement and Jim Crow
basis: Virginia's constitutional convention sat 12 Jun 1901 to 26 Jun 1902 expressly to disfranchise Black voters. Registered Black voters in Virginia fell from about 147,000 in 1900 to about 21,000 in 1904.
note: Sixty-three years. Opens with the 1902 constitution and closes with the Voting Rights Act. Pleasant Valley Cemetery was established in 1922, squarely inside this era - a separate burial ground is this era made physical, and it is the reason the project's Black records begin when they do.

label: Segregated schooling, Douglass era
basis: Douglass opens Sep 1941; Loudoun County public schools desegregated 1968, following Green v. New Kent County, 27 May 1968.
source: Douglass High School (Leesburg, VA); Encyclopedia Virginia, 'Massive Resistance'
note: Fourteen years after Brown. Loudoun did not act on its own - Green struck down 'freedom of choice' and large-scale desegregation began across Virginia that year.

label: Massive Resistance
basis: Byrd's call 25 Feb 1956; Stanley Plan 27 Aug 1956; school closings Sep 1958; both the federal district court and the Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals ruled the closings unconstitutional on 19 Jan 1959.
note: A short, sharp era nested inside the segregation band. Virginia closed public schools rather than desegregate them.
